title: The Stalk of Grass 2
content:
The rhythmic tapping of bamboo against cobblestone flickered in and out, teasing their ears from everywhere and nowhere at once. In this soup of a fog, pinpointing its direction was completely out of the question—let alone figuring out what kind of twisted thing was making the noise.

"Over here, everyone," Wei Wuxian called out softly. "Huddle up, keep tight. Nobody move, and whatever you do, don't draw your swords."

Blinded by this pea-soup mist, a bunch of jumpy teenagers blindly swinging live steel wouldn't scratch an enemy; they’d just end up skewering each other. A beat later, the tapping snapped to a dead halt. After an agonizing stretch of silence, one of the junior cultivators whispered, "It’s back... How long is that thing going to stalk us?!"

Wei Wuxian caught the phrase. "It’s been trailing you this whole time?"

"Ever since we entered the city," Lan Sizhui explained, keeping his voice low. "The mist was so thick we were terrified of getting separated, so we bunched up. That's when we first heard it. It wasn't nearly this fast back then—just a slow, plodding strike, over and over. We caught a glimpse of a short, scrawny figure shuffling through the white ahead, but the second we gave chase, it vanished. And after that... the tapping just glued itself to our heels."

"How short?" Wei Wuxian asked.

Lan Sizhui hovered a flat hand around his own chest. "Very short. Frail, too."

Wei Wuxian frowned. "How long have you been wandering inside the city walls?"

"A little under half an incense stick."

"Under half an incense stick?" Wei Wuxian turned toward the empty haze. "Hanguang-jun, how long have we been in?"

Lan Wangji’s voice cut through the milky gloom, calm and level: "Nearly a full stick."

"See that?" Wei Wuxian said. "We got here before you did. How could you possibly have ended up ahead of us? You shouldn't have run into us unless you doubled back."

Jin Ling couldn't keep his mouth shut any longer. "We didn't double back! We’ve been marching straight down this exact road the entire time!"

Both groups had been walking forward in a straight line, which meant only one thing: had someone tampered with the street, bending it into a looping phantom maze?

"Did anyone try sword-gliding up to scout the layout?" Wei Wuxian asked.

"I did," Lan Sizhui admitted. "It felt like I ascended for quite a while, but looking down, I barely gained any real altitude at all. Worse, there were shadowy shapes darting through the upper air. I wasn't sure what they were, and with no backup in sight, I didn't want to push my luck, so I dropped back down."

A heavy, uneasy silence swallowed the group. Eastern Shu was notorious for damp valleys and heavy mountain fog, so they hadn't thought twice about the mist when they first crossed into Yi City. Looking at it now, this was no trick of the weather—they were breathing cursed demonic vapor.

Lan Jingyi went pale. "Wait, is this fog poisonous?!"

"Doesn't seem like it," Wei Wuxian replied casually. "We’ve been marinating in it for a while now, and nobody's dropped dead yet."

Jin Ling clicked his tongue in bitter regret. "If I’d known, I would've brought Fairy with me. It’s all that damn donkey’s fault!"

Wei Wuxian’s shoulders instantly broke out in goosebumps at the dog’s name, but before he could react, Lan Jingyi fired back, "Don’t you dare pin this on our donkey! Your dog was the one that snapped first! Little Apple just gave it a well-deserved kick to the snout—who's really to blame here? Now neither of them can walk, so you're even!"

Wei Wuxian’s head snapped around. "Wait, what?! A dog bit my Little Apple?!"

"As if that stubborn farm beast can compare to my spiritual hound!" Jin Ling scoffed. "Fairy was a personal gift from my youngest uncle! If anything happens to him, a ten-thousand-donkey herd couldn't pay off the debt!"

Wei Wuxian fired right back, completely making things up as he went: "Stop dropping Lianfang-zun's name to throw your weight around! My Little Apple was a personal gift from Hanguang-jun himself! Who gave you kids permission to haul my mount out on a night-hunt anyway? And look at what you did—you got him injured!"

The chorus of Lan disciples chorused in instant, scandalized unison: "Liar!" They refused to believe that someone with Hanguang-jun’s pristine, elevated taste would ever look twice at a mangy spotted donkey, let alone gift one away. Even if Lan Wangji himself didn't speak up to deny it, they were rejecting the theory on principle.

Lan Sizhui cleared his throat, deeply apologetic. "Um... My apologies, Young Master Mo. Your Little App... your donkey wouldn't stop braying around the Cloud Recesses. The clan elders had been lodging noise complaints for days and explicitly ordered us to chase it off the mountain during this night-hunt, so we kind of..."

Jin Ling sneered, equally unconvinced. "I want to kick that beast every time I look at it. And 'Little Apple'? What a brainless, tacky name."

Lan Jingyi, meanwhile, was suddenly terrified that the donkey might actually have been a gift from Hanguang-jun after all. Scrambling to smooth things over, he rushed to its defense: "What’s wrong with 'Little Apple'? It loves apples, so it’s called Little Apple! It’s down-to-earth and honest. That name beats calling a pampered, chubby mutt 'Fairy' by a hundred miles!"

"Fairy is not fat!" Jin Ling bristled, his face turning red. "Show me a single spiritual hound leaner or faster than him—"

The air snapped shut. Total, dead silence.

After a few seconds of nothing, Wei Wuxian cautiously called out, "Anyone still there?"

A wave of muffled, desperate groaning echoed from all around them—mmph, mmph, nggh!—confirming that yes, everyone was still accounted for.

Lan Wangji’s voice drifted out of the mist, cold as ice: "Clamoring."

He had silenced the entire pack in one fell swoop. Wei Wuxian subconsciously touched his own lips, letting out a silent, relieved breath. Dodged a bullet there.

Right on cue, heavy footsteps dragged through the white mist to their left.

It was an awkward, stumbling shuffle, clumsy and agonizingly slow. Then came another from dead ahead, one from the right, and more shuffling footsteps closing in from behind and the flanks. The haze was too thick to make out silhouettes, but the rancid stench of rot and spoiled meat came rolling in on the breeze.

Wei Wuxian wasn't about to lose sleep over a handful of low-level walking corpses. Putting two fingers to his lips, he loosed a crisp, rising whistle that carried a clear command to retreat. Hearing the note, the stumbling figures beyond the fog hesitated, grinding to a momentary halt.

Then, without warning, they lunged forward in a manic frenzy!

Wei Wuxian froze. The command had completely backfired—instead of repelling them, it had whipped them into a bloodthirsty frenzy! And he knew for a fact he hadn't mixed up the calls; there was zero chance he’d ever confuse a "retreat" command with a "strike" order!

There was no time to dissect the mistake. Seven or eight lurching silhouettes burst through the milky curtain. With how dense the fog hung in Yi City, being able to make out their outlines meant they were practically on top of them!

A brilliant arc of icy blue light sliced through the white. Bichen cleared its scabbard in a heartbeat, whistling through the air in a lethal, sweeping perimeter that sheared several walking corpses clean in half at the waist before snapping back into its sheath. Wei Wuxian exhaled, but Lan Wangji’s voice came low and sharp: "Why?"

Wei Wuxian was racking his brain over the exact same question. Why did the whistle fail to herd them? They moved with a slow, clumsy stagger and reeked of grave rot—definitely bottom-tier walking corpses, the kind he could usually scatter with two claps of his hands. It made no sense for his technique to suddenly glitch; it didn't even rely on spiritual energy. Something like this had never happened...

A chilling realization struck him, and a cold sweat broke out along his spine.

No. That wasn't true. It had happened before—more than once, in fact. There was indeed one specific breed of corpse he could never override.

Fierce corpses already locked under the absolute dominion of the Yin Tiger Tally!

Lan Wangji lifted the Silence Spell, and Lan Sizhui’s panicked voice spilled out immediately: "Hanguang-jun, is the danger escalating? Should we evacuate the city right now?"

"We can't," another boy whined. "The mist is blinding, the streets loop in circles, and we can't fly out..."

One of the other juniors gasped, "Wait, I think more of them are coming!"

"Where? I don't hear any footsteps!"

"I... I think I hear breathing..." The kid realized how idiotic that sounded the second the words left his mouth and clamped his jaws shut.

Another boy scoffed, "Are you out of your mind? Breathing? Walking corpses are dead meat—how could a corpse breathe?"

Before the scoff could finish, a hulking silhouette plowed straight toward them. Bichen flashed once more, lopping the monster’s head from its shoulders with clean precision. But as the blade connected, a bizarre, wet spitting sound erupted from the severed neck. The boys standing closest shrieked in horror.

Fearing they’d been struck, Wei Wuxian called out, "What happened?!"

"Something sprayed out of its neck!" Lan Jingyi cried. "Some kind of powder—it tastes horribly bitter, sweet, and disgusting all at once! Pah! Pah!" Poor kid had opened his mouth at the worst possible moment and swallowed a mouthful of the flying grime, spitting wildly with zero regard for Lan clan decorum.

Whatever sprayed from a walking corpse was bad news. With the tainted dust still hanging thick in the air, breathing it deep into their lungs was infinitely worse than getting a mouthful of it.

"Get back from that spot, all of you!" Wei Wuxian barked. "Jingyi, over here, let me look at you."

"Coming," Jingyi grumbled. "Where are you? I can't see a damn thing!"

It was literally impossible to see your own hand in front of your face. Remembering how Bichen’s spiritual glow always pierced straight through the murk, Wei Wuxian turned to his flank. "Hanguang-jun, draw your steel for a second so he has a light to follow."

The figure standing shoulder-to-shoulder beside him gave no answer, nor did he move an inch.

Suddenly, seven paces to his right, a radiant, icy blue blade lit up the fog.

...If Lan Wangji was over there...

Then who the hell had been standing silently at his left elbow this entire time?!

Before Wei Wuxian could react, the world went dark. A shadowy, pitch-black face leaned in close, looming right over his nose.

The face was black because it was choked beneath a swirling vortex of dense, oily dark mist!

A gloved hand shot out, snatching the Qiankun pouch hanging from Wei Wuxian's sash. The second fingers made contact, the pouch ballooned violently. The drawstring snapped, and three furious, writhing dark spirits erupted from the cloth, lunging straight for the thief's throat with shrieking malice!

Wei Wuxian chuckled. "Looking to swipe the evil-binding pouch? You might want to get your eyes checked, friend—what are you doing grabbing my spirit-trapping pouch instead?"

Ever since they had wrestled the corpse's torso away from the mysterious gravedigger back at the Chang Clan cemetery in Yueyang, Wei Wuxian and Lan Wangji had stayed on high alert. They knew the culprit wouldn't swallow that loss lying down and would tail them, waiting for a chance to strike. Sure enough, the moment they stepped into the confusing, crowded mess of Yi City, the gravedigger had tried to make his move under the cover of the fog. He’d certainly caught his target—it was just too bad Wei Wuxian had swapped the pouch holding the left arm with an ordinary spirit-trapping pouch hours ago.

With a sharp ring of steel, the stranger backflipped into the haze, drawing his sword. A chorus of shrieks followed as the dark spirits were sheared apart by a vicious, sweeping arc.

High-level cultivation, Wei Wuxian noted mentally. He didn't waste a breath: "Hanguang-jun! Our gravedigger’s here!"

No warning was necessary. Lan Wangji’s keen ears had already mapped the ambush. Without a word, Bichen shot through the mist like a flying shuttle, trailing razor-sharp sword aura straight for the intruder.

The playing field, however, was heavily skewed. The gravedigger’s blade was cloaked in black fog, suppressing its spiritual glow and making it virtually invisible in the white murk. Lan Wangji’s Bichen, by contrast, blazed with unmistakable brilliance. Lan Wangji was standing in the open while the enemy struck from the dark. Worse, the intruder’s swordsmanship was exceptionally refined, and he clearly knew the Gusu Lan sword forms inside and out. In a blind brawl through heavy fog, the stranger could slash indiscriminately, while Lan Wangji had to hold his strikes back to keep from clipping the kids.

The ring of crossing blades came fast and furious. Wei Wuxian heard the dull thud of steel biting into flesh, his heart seizing as he blurted out, "Lan Zhan?! Did he hit you?!"

A muffled grunt drifted back from the fog, sounding like someone taking a clean blow to a vital point—definitely not Lan Wangji's voice.

Lan Wangji’s cool response drifted over: "As if."

Wei Wuxian grinned. "Right on!"

A low, bitter scoff sounded from the stranger before the swords collided again. The radiant glow of Bichen and the clash of steel gradually receded into the distance; Wei Wuxian knew Lan Wangji was intentionally pulling the fight away from the clearing to give the kids breathing room, leaving the rest of the mess squarely on his shoulders.

Turning back to the disciples, he called out, "How are the ones who breathed the powder holding up?"

Lan Sizhui’s voice shook. "They... they can barely stand!"

"Huddle in the center! Sound off, give me a headcount!"

Mercifully, with the walking corpses cut down and the gravedigger baited away, nothing else crept out of the dark. Even that creepy bamboo tapping hadn't chimed back in to cause trouble. The remaining disciples gathered into a tight circle, counting off—every single head accounted for.

Wei Wuxian pulled Lan Jingyi over, pressing a hand to the boy's forehead. Feverish. He touched the brows of the other boys who’d caught a lungful of the spray; identical burning heat.

Prying Jingyi's eyelid back, Wei Wuxian ordered, "Stick your tongue out. Say 'ah'."

"Ah."

"Mm. Congratulations. You've been poisoned with corpse powder."

Jin Ling snapped, "What the hell is there to congratulate?!"

Wei Wuxian shrugged. "It’s a character-building experience. Great story to tell when you're old."

Normally, you only caught corpse poisoning if a ghoul bit you, clawed you, or if their rotted, infected blood seeped into an open wound. It was almost unheard of for an active cultivator to let a shambling corpse get close enough to sink its teeth into them, which meant nobody ever bothered packing corpse-poison remedies on a routine night-hunt.

Lan Sizhui asked anxiously, "Young Master Mo, is it fatal?"

"Not yet," Wei Wuxian replied breezy. "Give it time to seep into the bloodstream, spread through the vessels, and reach the heart, and then you're done for."

Sizhui swallowed hard. "What... what happens then?"

"Whatever happens to a corpse happens to you. Best-case scenario, you rot into mush. Worst-case, you sprout a lovely coat of white fuzz, turn into a stiff, and spend the rest of eternity hopping everywhere on two legs."

A collective gasp of sheer horror swept through the poisoned boys.

Wei Wuxian raised an eyebrow. "Want it cured?"

Nods flew like a flock of woodpeckers.

Wei Wuxian pointed a finger. "Then listen closely: from this second onward, every single one of you does exactly as I say. No exceptions."

A good chunk of these kids didn't even know who this weird guy was. But seeing that he could casually banter with Hanguang-jun on equal footing, act intimately with him, and even address the esteemed master by his birth name—paired with the fact that they were stranded in a foggy, haunted town with their veins burning with deadly poison—they instinctively reached for any lifeline they could get. Besides, there was an effortless, almost arrogant confidence in the way he carried himself that naturally took the wheel.

They chorused in unison: "Understood!"

Wei Wuxian pressed his advantage. "You jump when I say jump, and you don't talk back. Got it?"

"Got it!"

Wei Wuxian clapped his hands. "On your feet! Unpoisoned disciples carry the poisoned ones—hoist them over your shoulders if you can. If you carry them flat, keep their heads and chests tilted up."

Lan Jingyi grumbled, "I can still walk! Why do I need to be carried?"

"Big brother," Wei Wuxian sighed, "if you go running around, your pulse spikes, your blood pumps faster, and that poison rushes straight for your heart twice as fast. Keep your movement to an absolute minimum. Better yet, play dead."

The poisoned boys went rigid as planks on the spot, letting their peers hoist them up. One of the kids perched on his martial brother's back muttered under his breath, "I swear... that corpse that blew the dust really was breathing."

The boy lugging him panted under the weight, snapping, "I told you, if it breathes, it's alive!"

Lan Sizhui adjusted his grip on his companion. "Young Master Mo, we're all set. Where are we heading?"

Lan Sizhui really is the most sensible, well-behaved kid in the whole lot, Wei Wuxian thought warmly. Aloud, he said, "Getting out of the city is off the table for now. We go knocking on doors."

Jin Ling frowned. "Knocking on what?"

Wei Wuxian deadpanned, "Aside from houses, what else in this town has a door?"

"You want us to go inside those houses?!" Jin Ling protested. "The street is already a death trap—who knows what kind of sick monsters are lurking behind those walls watching us?!"

The second he voiced the thought, the dark seemed to press in closer. It felt as though dozens of unseen eyes were genuinely peering through the fog and cracked shutters, tracking their every breath. A cold shiver crawled up everyone's arms.

"Fair point," Wei Wuxian admitted cheerfully. "It’s hard to say whether it's deadlier out here or worse inside. But out here is already a disaster, so inside can't get much worse. Move along, clock's ticking—we need to purge that poison."

Left with no other choice, the group followed his lead. Per Wei Wuxian's strict orders, each boy kept one hand firmly gripped onto the scabbard of the person in front of them to avoid drifting apart in the murk, moving house to house and rapping on the wood.

Jin Ling hammered on a doorframe for half a minute without hearing a peep. "Seems empty. Let's head in."

Wei Wuxian’s voice floated back from down the line: "Who told you to go barging into empty houses? Keep knocking. We need a place with living people."

Jin Ling threw his hands up. "You're specifically looking for people?!"

"Yup. And knock properly—you were slamming that wood like a debt collector. Show some manners."

Jin Ling looked ready to kick the door off its hinges, but after glaring at the wood, he merely stomped his foot against the pavers in bitter defeat.

Every single shopfront along the main road was shuttered tight, deaf to their knocking. Jin Ling grew more irritated by the second, though his knocks noticeably softened. Lan Sizhui, on the other hand, remained calm and patient throughout. Coming up to the thirteenth storefront, he repeated the exact same polite phrase he’d spoken twelve times before: "Excuse me, is anyone home?"

Creak.

The door shifted. A narrow black seam opened up.

The interior was pitch-black, offering no view of what lay beyond, and whoever had pulled the latch didn't say a word. The boys standing nearest instinctively took a half-step back.

Lan Sizhui steadied his breathing. "Pardon the intrusion... Are you the shopkeeper?"

After an agonizing beat, a raspy, ancient voice creaked through the crack: "Aye."

Wei Wuxian stepped up, clapping Sizhui on the shoulder to guide him back. "Shopkeeper, we're travelers passing through your town. The fog was so thick we lost our bearings, and after walking for hours, we're quite exhausted. Would you be so kind as to let us rest our feet inside your shop for a moment?"

The eerie voice scraped back: "My shop ain't meant for resting."

Wei Wuxian acted as though that was the most normal response in the world. "None of the other shops seem to have anyone home. Won't you do us a small favor? We’ll compensate you handsomely."

Jin Ling couldn't resist scoffing: "Where would you get the coin for a handsome reward? Just so you know, I'm not lending you a copper."

Wei Wuxian pulled out an exquisitely embroidered money pouch, dangling it in front of the boy's nose. "See this? What does it look like?"

Lan Jingyi gasped in horror. "You have some nerve! That belongs to Hanguang-jun!"

Right in the middle of their squabble, the door creaked open a fraction wider. The interior remained obscured, but they could finally see the figure standing behind the threshold: an old woman with a head of coarse, salt-and-pepper hair, her face blank and expressionless.

Though she was severely hunched over and looked ancient at first glance, she didn't actually have that many wrinkles or age spots; you could almost pass her off as a middle-aged matron. She pulled the door wide and stepped aside, apparently willing to grant them shelter.

Jin Ling was genuinely stunned, whispering, "She's actually letting us in?"

"Of course she is," Wei Wuxian whispered back with an easy smirk. "I wedged my boot straight into the doorframe—she couldn't shut it if she tried. If she hadn't let us in, I was kicking it off its hinges anyway."

Jin Ling stared at him in deadpan disbelief.

Yi City was already dripping with foul, uncanny air, and anyone living here was definitely far from ordinary. Looking at this creepy old woman had the disciples’ guts twisting into knots. They were thoroughly repulsed by the idea of stepping across that threshold, but caught between a rock and a hard place, they had to gamble. Hoisting their stiff, poisoned companions, they shuffled into the dark parlor one by one. The old woman watched them with cold, dead eyes, slamming the door shut the second the last boy crossed over.

Pitch-black darkness swallowed the room once more.

"Shopkeeper, why keep the lanterns dark?" Wei Wuxian called out.

"Lantern’s on the table," the old woman wheezed. "Light it yourselves."

Lan Sizhui happened to be standing right beside a wooden table. Groping through the gloom, his fingers brushed against a cold ceramic oil lamp, coming away coated in a thick layer of greasy dust. Slipping a fire talisman from his sleeve, he blew a spark to ignite the paper.

He leaned down to touch the flame to the wick, his eyes casually flicking across the room.

In that split second, an icy jolt shot from the soles of his feet straight to the crown of his skull, turning his scalp instantly numb.

The entire parlor was crammed wall to wall, shoulder to shoulder, packed with a sea of silent figures—every single one of them staring back at him with wide, unblinking eyes!
